Abstract
This study proposes a domestic edge computing terminal pest identification system based on large model compres-
sion and lightweight technology, integrating new algorithms based on Transformer and ConvLSTM, and optimizing its 
performance in resource-constrained environments through adaptive deployment strategies. By evaluating the perfor-
mance of four different models (Transformer ConvLSTM, CNN, LSTM and Transformer) in terms of recognition accuracy, 
inference speed, computing resource consumption and adaptive deployment effect, this study reveals the advantages 
and disadvantages of each model in edge computing tasks. The model based on Transformer ConvLSTM performed 
best in recognition accuracy, reaching 94.5%, significantly better than other models; while the CNN model was the most 
efficient in inference speed, reaching 52 frames per second (FPS). The adaptive deployment strategy of the Transformer 
ConvLSTM model, the Transformer ConvLSTM model can dynamically adjust the model complexity to effectively cope 
with higher computing resource requirements, thereby improving inference speed and reducing resource consumption. 
On resource-constrained devices, the optimized Transformer ConvLSTM model can maintain high recognition accuracy 
and significantly reduce latency. Although the compression strategy slightly affects the accuracy, it greatly improves the 
inference speed, especially in the CNN model.
Highlights
•	 Innovative hybrid model design: It is proposed to combine Transformer with ConvLSTM to design an efficient pest 
recognition model that can capture global information and temporal features at the same time. Transformer handles 
long-distance dependencies, while ConvLSTM better handles spatiotemporal data. This fusion enhances the adapt-
ability and robustness of the model in dynamic agricultural environments.
•	 Lightweight optimization technology: Through optimization through model quantization, pruning, and knowledge 
distillation, the model can effectively reduce computing and storage requirements while maintaining high accuracy, 
making it adaptable to resource-constrained edge computing devices.
•	 Adaptive deployment strategy: It proposes an adaptive deployment strategy that dynamically adjusts the model com-
plexity and computing accuracy, optimizes the model deployment in real time according to the hardware resources 
and network conditions of the edge device, and ensures that the system can achieve optimal performance in different 
environments.

1  Introduction
With the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence, the integration of edge computing into various intelligent terminals 
has become a prominent research focus [1, 2]. In particular, the development of pest identification systems in agricul-
ture has emerged as a crucial technology for enhancing crop management efficiency and minimizing pesticide usage. 
Traditional image recognition methods typically rely on cloud computing, which, although advantageous in terms of 
computational power, faces significant challenges in practical applications. These challenges include network latency, 
bandwidth limitations, and data privacy concerns. In contrast, edge computing, as an emerging computing architec-
ture, provides a more efficient and real-time solution [3]. By shifting computation from the cloud to edge devices, edge 
computing enables data processing to occur closer to the source, thereby significantly reducing transmission delays, 
improving real-time performance, and mitigating issues related to data privacy and bandwidth [4].
As a novel computing architecture, edge computing offers a more efficient and real-time solution by shifting 
computing tasks from the cloud to the device side. This approach enables data processing closer to the source, sig-
nificantly reducing data transmission delays, enhancing real-time performance, and addressing issues related to data 
privacy and bandwidth limitations. In the context of agricultural pest identification systems, traditional rule-based 
methods and shallow learning algorithms often struggle to adapt to the complexities of environmental variability 
and the diversity of pest species [5]. In recent years, significant progress has been made in the application of deep 
learning, especially convolutional neural networks (CNN), in image recognition. However, these methods often have 
large computational requirements and models, making it difficult to deploy on resource constrained edge devices 
[6]. Therefore, how to ensure the recognition accuracy while optimizing the calculation efficiency has become an 
urgent problem in the application of edge computing [7].
In order to achieve efficient pest recognition, this paper proposes a new algorithm based on Transformer and 
ConvLSTM, combined with large model compression and lightweight technology, and designs an optimized pest 
recognition system suitable for domestic edge computing terminals [8]. This system innovatively combines the long 
sequence modeling capability of Transformer with the spatiotemporal feature extraction capability of ConvLSTM, 
which not only improves the recognition accuracy, but also optimizes the computational efficiency, making it more 
suitable for deployment on resource-constrained edge devices [9]. Specifically, the Transformer module effectively 
captures the long-range dependencies in the image through the self-attention mechanism, thereby enhancing the 
recognition ability of pests in complex environments [10]; while the ConvLSTM module extracts spatiotemporal 
dynamic features by modeling image sequences, further improving the adaptability and robustness of the system 
in dynamic environments [11].
In order to solve the computing and storage limitations of edge devices, this paper proposes a large model com-
pression and lightweight method based on pruning, quantization and knowledge distillation [12], which reduces 
the computing and storage requirements without significantly reducing the model accuracy, thereby improving the 
system’s operating efficiency [13, 14]. In addition, in view of the heterogeneity and dynamic resource changes of 
edge devices, this paper designs an adaptive deployment strategy that can dynamically adjust model deployment 
according to device hardware configuration and network environment, ensuring that high-precision models are 
used for identification when computing resources are sufficient, and lightweight models are used for fast reasoning 
when resources are limited.
In practical applications, the pest recognition system proposed in this paper can not only identify various agri-
cultural pests in real time and accurately, provide farmers with timely prevention and control suggestions, thereby 
improving crop management efficiency [15, 16], but also support automated pesticide spraying and precision agri-
cultural management through collaboration with agricultural IoT devices [17]. Compared with traditional cloud-based 
pest recognition methods, edge computing systems avoid network delays, can better protect user privacy, and pro-
vide reference significance for intelligent agricultural applications. The innovation of this work is not only reflected 
in the fusion of Transformer and ConvLSTM, but also in the proposed adaptive deployment strategy, which enables 
the system to achieve optimal performance on a variety of edge computing devices and expand its application scope 
in a variety of agricultural environments.

2  Related work
2.1  Applications and challenges of edge computing terminals
Edge computing technology, by transferring computing and data storage from the cloud to the edge of the network, 
has been widely used in smart home, intelligent transportation, industrial Internet of Things and other fields [18, 19]. 
Especially in the agricultural field, the application of edge computing has significant advantages, because it can reduce 
the delay of data transmission and improve the real-time processing ability [19, 20]. This is crucial for agricultural pest 
identification systems, as pest identification not only requires high accuracy, but also real-time feedback for farmers to 
make timely decisions, thereby reducing pesticide use and increasing crop yields. However, edge computing terminals 
are usually limited by hardware resources and have weak processing capacity, which puts forward higher requirements 
for efficient computing and reasonable scheduling of storage resources [21, 22]. To address this challenge, research-
ers have proposed various technical solutions, such as large model compression and lightweight technology, aimed 
at reducing the computational and storage requirements of the model while maintaining high recognition accuracy.
In edge computing terminals, due to limited hardware resources, how to optimize the performance of the model 
while ensuring efficient computing has become the core issue of technology development [23]. In order to address this 
challenge, research in recent years has focused on the compression and lightweighting of large models, among which 
pruning, quantization, and knowledge distillation methods have become mainstream technologies [24]. These methods 
can improve computational efficiency and adapt to resource limitations of edge devices without significantly reducing 
model accuracy by reducing redundant calculations and parameter quantities [25, 26]. However, the implementation of 
these technologies often comes with losses during the model training process, and how to compress the model while 
maximizing its performance has become the key to further optimization. The heterogeneity and dynamic resource 
changes of edge computing terminals are also a major challenge in practical applications. Edge devices often have sig-
nificant differences in computing power and storage space, and the resources of these devices may change at any time, 
requiring the system to be able to adaptively adjust under different device and environmental conditions [27]. Therefore, 
scholars have proposed some adaptive deployment strategies that can dynamically adjust the complexity and inference 
accuracy of the model based on real-time changes in hardware resources and network environment [28]. For example, 
when the computing resources of the device are sufficient, the system can adopt more accurate deep learning models, 
while when the device resources are limited, it automatically switches to lightweight models to ensure that the system 
can always run at the optimal resource level [29]. At present, the application of new algorithms based on Transformer and 
ConvLSTM in pest recognition has shown significant advantages. Transformer can effectively capture long-range depend-
encies in images through its self attention mechanism, enhancing its ability to recognize pests in complex backgrounds 
[30]. ConvLSTM further enhances the adaptability and robustness of the system in dynamic environments by extracting 
spatiotemporal dynamic features. Combining these two technologies can fully leverage their respective advantages 
and improve the overall performance of the model. However, such deep learning models typically require significant 
computational resources, which presents additional challenges for edge devices. In order to effectively run this complex 
model that combines Transformer and ConvLSTM on edge devices, researchers have introduced model compression and 
lightweighting techniques. These techniques can significantly reduce computational and storage requirements while 
maintaining high recognition accuracy by optimizing the structure of the model, quantifying parameters, and prun-
ing. Specifically, pruning techniques can remove redundant parameters in the model, quantization techniques reduce 
computational complexity by reducing parameter accuracy, and knowledge distillation techniques further improve the 
performance of small models by transferring knowledge from large models to small models. By combining these tech-
nologies, not only has the computational efficiency of the model been optimized, but the system has also been able to 
run efficiently on resource constrained edge devices [31]. In addition to model compression, another key challenge in 
edge computing applications is how to design adaptive deployment strategies to cope with the hardware configuration 
and resource fluctuations of different devices [32, 33].

ognition methods based on deep learning have gradually made significant progress. Especially the application of

learning models usually require large computing resources and storage space, which makes them difficult to be 
directly applied to resource constrained edge computing devices. In agricultural production, edge devices often 
need to work in offline or low bandwidth environments. Therefore, how to optimize deep learning models to adapt 
to the capabilities of these devices has become an important direction of current research.
In order to overcome this challenge, research in recent years has focused on the application of large model compression 
and lightweight technology to improve the operational efficiency of models and reduce their computational and storage 
requirements [34]. Specifically, pruning, quantification, and knowledge distillation techniques are widely used in the optimiza-
tion of deep learning models. Pruning technology reduces the size and computational complexity of the model by removing 
redundant connections or neurons in the network; Quantization reduces the accuracy of network weights, thereby lowering 
computational complexity; Knowledge distillation involves transferring knowledge from a large model to a small model, 
allowing the small model to maintain high accuracy while reducing computational and storage costs. The combination of 
these technologies enables deep learning models that originally required high computing resources to run efficiently on edge 
devices. In response to the limitations of traditional convolutional neural networks and long short-term memory networks 
in processing spatiotemporal data, new algorithms based on Transformer and ConvLSTM have gradually gained attention 
in recent years. Transformer, with its powerful self attention mechanism, can effectively capture long-range dependencies 
in images, thereby enhancing the ability to recognize pests in complex backgrounds [35]. ConvLSTM combines the local 
feature extraction capability of convolutional neural networks with the advantages of LSTM in temporal data processing, 
effectively extracting spatiotemporal features in dynamic environments, thereby improving the system’s adaptability and 
robustness to environmental changes [36]. These two models have their own advantages, and their combination can further 
improve the accuracy and stability of pest identification. However, although the algorithms based on Transformer and Con-
vLSTM have made significant progress in recognition effect, they still have a high demand for computing resources, which 
poses additional challenges for the application of edge computing devices [37]. In order to achieve real-time operation of 
these complex models on resource constrained edge devices, researchers have proposed various model compression and 
lightweight techniques. For example, simplifying the Transformer structure, reducing its number of layers, or using low rank 
decomposition techniques can significantly reduce computational complexity; The structural optimization of ConvLSTM 
can also alleviate computational pressure by reducing the depth of convolutional layers and the number of parameters in 
LSTM units [38]. How to dynamically adjust computing strategies based on the hardware resources of different edge devices 
while optimizing the model has also become an important research direction. Edge computing devices often have different 
computing power and storage space, and these resources may change at any time. Therefore, how to achieve efficient adap-
tive deployment on these heterogeneous devices has become a key issue in technological development. Therefore, scholars 
have proposed an adaptive deployment strategy based on dynamic model adjustment, which can automatically select the 
appropriate model complexity and computational accuracy according to the real-time changes in the computing resources 
of edge devices and network environment. For example, on devices with sufficient computing resources, high-precision deep 
learning models can be used; On devices with limited resources, it is possible to automatically switch to lightweight models 
to ensure efficient system operation [39]. The core goal of the adaptive deployment strategy is to achieve the best match 
between the edge computing device and the model, and ensure that the model can be automatically optimized according 
to the hardware configuration and operating environment of the device. This strategy can not only improve recognition 
accuracy, but also effectively reduce the waste of computing resources, improve the overall performance and response speed 
of the system [40]. For example, in the agricultural production process, the pest identification system based on edge comput-
ing can adjust the calculation resource allocation of the model according to the real-time environment changes of farmland, 
so as to ensure that the system can always maintain a good recognition effect under different conditions [41]. Researchers 
are gradually overcoming these challenges by employing model compression techniques, such as pruning, quantization, 
and knowledge distillation, which aim to reduce the size and computational requirements of these models. Additionally, 
lightweight network architectures have been developed, where more efficient layers and components replace traditional 
ones to minimize the computational burden without compromising accuracy. These efforts are further complemented by 
adaptive deployment strategies, which dynamically adjust the model’s complexity and resource consumption based on the 
specific hardware and environmental conditions of the edge device. As a result, edge computing terminal pest identification 
systems are becoming increasingly efficient and accurate. These advances not only enhance pest management efficiency in 
agricultural production but also have broader applications for intelligent recognition systems in other Internet of Things (IoT) 
environments, such as smart cities, autonomous vehicles, and environmental monitoring. By analyzing the practical feasibility

3  System architecture and algorithm design
3.1  Overall system architecture
The overall architecture of this system is designed to achieve efficient identification of pests in agricultural environment by 
integrating a new algorithm based on Transformer ConvLSTM [43], and can be deployed adaptively on edge computing ter-
minals. The system consists of four main parts: data acquisition module, preprocessing module, pest identification module, 
and result output module, as shown in Fig. 1.
Specifically, the data acquisition module is responsible for collecting real-time image data in farmland through sensors, 
and then transmitting the image data to the edge computing terminal through wireless communication as the original input 
of subsequent recognition tasks [44]. The preprocessing module performs denoising, enhancement, and other operations 
on the collected raw images, using filtering algorithms such as Gaussian Filtering and Histogram Equalization to improve 
image quality and details, ensuring the effectiveness of subsequent recognition algorithms.
In the pest identification module, a hybrid model based on Transformer and ConvLSTM plays a crucial role in processing 
and analyzing data. The Transformer model utilizes a self-attention mechanism to capture both local and global spatiotem-
poral features of pests in images. By focusing on the relationships between different regions in the image, the Transformer 
enhances the ability to identify and recognize pests with greater accuracy, even in complex backgrounds. The ConvLSTM 
module, on the other hand, specializes in handling sequential data by modeling the temporal changes of pests across frames, 
effectively capturing dynamic variations over time [45].
In terms of data transmission and interaction between modules, the system adopts a well-defined mechanism to ensure 
the smooth flow of information while maintaining security and real-time performance. Each module exchanges data through 
secure communication channels, employing encryption protocols such as SSL/TLS to protect sensitive data during transmis-
sion. Moreover, to guarantee real-time processing, data is transmitted in small, manageable packets that minimize latency. 
The interaction between Transformer and ConvLSTM models is facilitated by a shared intermediate representation of the 
pest data, which is updated at each time step to ensure that both spatial and temporal features are effectively utilized.
Additionally, the system incorporates an adaptive architecture that can dynamically adjust the model’s complexity and 
resource demands based on the available hardware of edge computing devices. This adjustment is based on factors such 
as computational power, memory, and storage capacity. By scaling the model appropriately, the system ensures efficient 
deployment without compromising processing speed or recognition accuracy. Through this approach, the system not only 
ensures secure and real-time data transmission but also guarantees optimal performance across various edge devices with 
differing resource constraints.

In traditional deep learning methods, Transformer and ConvLSTM are each applied to different types of data and 
tasks, and the two are complementary. Transformer is good at processing tasks with long-distance dependencies, 
especially in global feature extraction in natural language processing and image processing; while ConvLSTM focuses 
on capturing the spatial–temporal features of time series data, and is particularly suitable for processing time series 
and dynamic image data. Transformer can capture global contextual information in images through the self-attention 
mechanism, and effectively solve the long-term dependencies between different regions. For example, in an agri-
cultural environment, pests may be distributed over a large area, and Transformer can understand the relationship 
between pests in different image regions, regardless of whether they are far from the center of the image. This gives 
Transformer a significant advantage in processing scenes with complex backgrounds and large scale changes. In 
contrast, ConvLSTM combines the spatial feature extraction capabilities of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) 
and the ability of LSTMs to process time series data, and is particularly suitable for capturing time series dynamic 
features in image sequences. In agricultural pest identification, the dynamic behavior of pests or their performance 
at different time points is crucial. ConvLSTM can effectively track the movement and changes of pests, especially in 
the processing of time series data in videos or multi-frame images.
In this study, the integration of Transformer and ConvLSTM is not just a simple juxtaposition, but an innovative 
combination through complementary advantages and functional fusion. First, Transformer is good at extracting 
global features, while ConvLSTM is good at processing time series data and space–time features. In this system, 
Transformer first captures the global contextual information in the image through the self-attention mechanism, 
such as the distribution and positional relationship of pests in a large range. Then, ConvLSTM processes the image 
sequence and analyzes the dynamic changes of pests in the time dimension, such as the activity trajectory and 
posture changes of pests. In this way, the model can not only capture the spatial features in static images, but also 
process the temporal changes of pest behavior, enhancing the dynamic adaptability of the system. The global infor-
mation provided by Transformer ensures that the model can accurately identify the location and type of pests even 
under complex backgrounds or lighting changes.
The workflow of the entire model is divided into three stages: First, each frame of the input image is processed 
by the Transformer network, and the global context information is captured through the self-attention mechanism 
to identify the possible areas of pests. Secondly, the image sequence is further processed by ConvLSTM to capture 
the movement trajectory and morphological changes of pests at different times. Finally, the features extracted by 
Transformer and ConvLSTM are combined through a fusion strategy, and finally the classification layer generates the 
category and location prediction results of the pests. This fusion of global features and temporal features enables the 
model to fully utilize the advantages of both in complex agricultural environments and improve recognition accuracy.
By using Transformer for global spatial feature extraction and ConvLSTM for capturing temporal change informa-
tion, this integration method enables the model to handle spatial and temporal changes at the same time, which 
is particularly suitable for dynamic identification of pests in agricultural environments. In addition, this fusion also 
improves the robustness of the model, allowing it to operate stably under different backgrounds, lighting changes 
and other conditions, significantly improving recognition accuracy.

3.3  Model compression and lightweight method design
In order to realize the efficient deployment of a new algorithm based on Transformer ConvLSTM on edge computing 
terminals, this paper designs a comprehensive model compression and lightweight strategy, which aims to reduce the 
computational complexity and storage overhead, while maintaining high recognition accuracy. These methods mainly 
include quantification, pruning, knowledge distillation, and network structure optimization, using advanced mathemati-
cal models and formulas to ensure that the compressed model still has strong performance [46].
The model compression technology discussed in this article is a key component that enables the efficient deploy-
ment of the Transformer-ConvLSTM hybrid model on resource-constrained edge devices. This approach stands out for its 
combination of multiple advanced compression techniques—pruning, quantization, and knowledge distillation—which 
collectively offer superior results compared to traditional methods that may use only one or two of these techniques. 
Pruning, for instance, effectively reduces the number of redundant connections in the neural network without significant

In order to address the challenges posed by the limited resources of edge computing devices, this paper introduces an

resources in real time. Specifically, the algorithm tracks CPU and GPU usage, memory consumption, and available storage, 
allowing the system to evaluate the current resource status of each device. Based on these measurements, the algorithm 
adjusts the model’s computational complexity and accuracy dynamically, ensuring that the model operates within the 
available resources without compromising performance.
The adjustment mechanism is governed by a set of predefined thresholds and a frequency control mechanism. The 
thresholds define the acceptable limits for each resource (e.g., CPU usage below 80%, memory usage under 75%), and

plexity adjustment involves scaling the model’s operations, such as reducing the depth or width of the model, simplifying 
layers, or performing quantization, based on the available resources.
Furthermore, the frequency of these adjustments is carefully calibrated to balance responsiveness with efficiency. 
For instance, the system might adjust every 5 s or upon detecting significant resource fluctuation, depending on the 
application requirements. The thresholds and frequency settings are flexible and can be fine-tuned for different types of 
edge devices and task scenarios. This ensures that the system can adaptively and efficiently deploy the model in a way 
that maximizes performance while minimizing computational load, especially in dynamic environments.

CPU usage on the Raspberry Pi 4 increased significantly during peak hours, rising from 60% during off-peak hours to 
78%. This spike was a consequence of the higher processing demands imposed by running multiple sensors and cam-
eras simultaneously. However, the system responded by adjusting the model’s complexity, helping to balance resource 
consumption despite the increased CPU load.
Memory usage also rose during peak hours, reaching 3.2 GB, as the system had to manage the additional data influx 
from the sensors and cameras. Despite this increase, memory usage remained within the Raspberry Pi 4’s available limits, 
demonstrating that the adaptive strategy effectively managed resources without overloading the system’s memory.
As shown in Table 12, the Jetson Xavier NX demonstrated consistently high recognition accuracy, maintaining 94% 
during peak hours and 95% during off-peak hours. This performance highlights the superior hardware capabilities of 
the device, enabling it to run the full model without significant degradation, even under high-load conditions. While the 
model complexity was adapted to balance resource consumption, the system consistently delivered robust accuracy, 
showcasing its capability to handle varying workloads. In terms of inference speed, the system maintained a stable rate 
of 32 FPS during peak hours, with a slight improvement to 38 FPS during off-peak hours. This modest increase reflects 
the system’s ability to optimize available resources during periods of lower demand. Even during peak hours, the Jetson 
Xavier NX outperformed the Raspberry Pi 4 in terms of FPS, underlining its ability to manage demanding tasks with 
minimal slowdowns.

When considering CPU usage, the Jetson Xavier NX remained more efficient than the Raspberry Pi 4, peaking at

due to the use of a more complex model. Despite this, the system effectively managed its memory resources, with 
only a slight decrease in memory usage during off-peak hours (4.8 GB). This adaptability in memory management 
further illustrates the Jetson Xavier NX’s ability to handle complex tasks without exceeding its available resources.
The adaptive deployment strategy was critical in ensuring that both devices could continue processing pest iden-
tification tasks despite fluctuating resource availability. Raspberry Pi 4, with its limited resources, required the most 
significant adjustment in model complexity, leading to noticeable drops in recognition accuracy and inference speed 
during peak hours. However, the system was still able to provide acceptable performance by reducing the model 
size, which allowed it to operate within the device’s constraints. In contrast, the NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX, being a 
high-performance device, was able to handle the full model during both peak and off-peak hours, maintaining high 
recognition accuracy and inference speed even during network congestion and sensor data influx. The adaptive 
strategy still optimized resource usage on the Jetson Xavier NX to ensure efficient operation, but its higher capacity 
allowed it to deliver better overall performance than the Raspberry Pi 4. The findings from both devices show how 
the adaptive deployment strategy can significantly improve the scalability and resource efficiency of AI models in 
real-time applications. While high-performance devices can maintain both accuracy and speed, low-resource devices 
like the Raspberry Pi 4 can still be optimized to provide adequate results, ensuring that pest identification tasks are 
effectively handled regardless of hardware limitations.
5  Conclusion
In this study, we propose a lightweight home edge computing terminal pest recognition system, leveraging the hybrid 
architecture of Transformer and ConvLSTM. The system’s efficacy in agricultural pest management has been experimen-
tally confirmed. Our findings indicate that the integrated Transformer-ConvLSTM model attains a recognition accuracy 
of 94.5%, markedly surpassing the traditional CNN (90.2%), LSTM (92.1%), and standalone Transformer (93.3%) models. 
The primary advantage of this model is its ability to capture global spatial dependencies via self-attention mechanisms, 
coupled with the convolutional long and short-term memory networks for modeling spatio-temporal dynamic features. 
This synergy significantly enhances the identification robustness for multi-scale pests in intricate farmland settings. To 
address the resource constraints inherent in edge devices, we introduce an innovative layered adaptive deployment strat-
egy. By dynamically fine-tuning model complexity and computational precision, we achieve an inference speed of 32 FPS 
on advanced devices like the NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX. This represents a 14% enhancement over our unoptimized model, 
while ensuring a real-time processing capability of 52 FPS. Additionally, through the incorporation of multi-dimensional 
compression techniques such as quantization, pruning, and knowledge distillation, we have reduced the model’s storage 
requirement by 70%, bringing it down to 300MB. CPU/memory usage is now limited to 65%/350MB, respectively. Prac-
tical deployment evaluations underscore the system’s superior performance in challenging backgrounds, adaptability 
to lighting variations, and energy efficiency. It offers rapid pest monitoring solutions tailored for precision agriculture. 
Nevertheless, our experiments highlight a decline in recognition rate to 85% in extremely low-light conditions (< 10 lx), 
suggesting areas for further research and optimization.

Abstract: This study proposes a domestic edge computing terminal pest identification system based on large model compres- sion and lightweight technology, integrating new algorithms based on Transformer and ConvLSTM, and optimizing its performance in resource-constrained environments through adaptive deployment strategies. By evaluating the perfor- mance of four different models (Transformer ConvLSTM, CNN, LSTM and Transformer) in terms of recognition accuracy, inference speed, computing resource consumption and adaptive deployment effect, this study reveals the advantages and disadvantages of each model in edge computing tasks. The model based on Transformer ConvLSTM performed best in recognition accuracy, reaching 94.5%, significantly better than other models; while the CNN model was the most efficient in inference speed, reaching 52 frames per second (FPS). The adaptive deployment strategy of the Transformer ConvLSTM model, the Transformer ConvLSTM model can dynamically adjust the model complexity to effectively cope with higher computing resource requirements, thereby improving inference speed and reducing resource consumption. On resource-constrained devices, the optimized Transformer ConvLSTM model can maintain high recognition accuracy and significantly reduce latency. Although the compression strategy slightly affects the accuracy, it greatly improves the inference speed, especially in the CNN model. Highlights • Innovative hybrid model design: It is proposed to combine Transformer with ConvLSTM to design an efficient pest recognition model that can capture global information and temporal features at the same time. Transformer handles long-distance dependencies, while ConvLSTM better handles spatiotemporal data.
